what_it_does: This paper describes a specialized analog chip for computing cross-correlations—a fundamental operation used by radar to measure distance and velocity, and by communication systems to find the start of received signals. Traditional digital approaches (converting the signal to numbers, then multiplying and adding using the main processor) are slow and power-hungry (only 5–20 TOPS per watt, meaning 5–20 trillion operations per joule of energy). This design uses analog compute cells—transistor pairs that perform multiplication directly in continuous current/voltage, not digital numbers—arranged in a 256 by 256 grid to compute 256 different time-shifted versions of the correlation in a single shot. The result: 1000 TOPS/W (50 times more efficient) and high compute density (1.3 TOPS per square millimeter of silicon).
